mcqs.question: A team creates a "UI Service," a "Business Logic Service," and a "Data Service," splitting along the technology stack. What is the main problem with this decomposition?
options: Almost every user action must hop across all three services, so nothing becomes independently deployable
It uses too many databases for a small system
It doesn't allow horizontal scaling of any of the three services
It requires a service mesh to function at all
mcqs.explanation: A layer-based split means one business action (like placing an order) crosses every layer-service, so the services can't actually deploy or scale independently — they're really one capability sliced by tech stack rather than business boundary. It doesn't inherently multiply databases, doesn't block horizontal scaling, and doesn't require a mesh.

mcqs.question: Two "independent" services both read and write the same underlying database table. What does this indicate?
options: The services are well-decomposed since they still have separate codebases
The services are actually coupled through shared data, and a schema change to one can silently break the other
This is a recommended pattern for keeping data consistent across services
It means the services need a service mesh to communicate safely
mcqs.explanation: Sharing a table means the services are coupled at the data layer regardless of having separate codebases — a schema change on one side can silently break the other, which is one of the two classic signs (along with chatty calls) that a boundary is wrong. It's not a recommended pattern, and a mesh addresses network traffic, not this data coupling.

mcqs.question: A team is unsure whether to start with a coarse-grained or fine-grained service split for a new system. What does the general guidance favor, and why?
options: Fine-grained from day one, since it's easier to merge services later than to split them
Coarse-grained first, since splitting an over-large service later is cheaper than merging services that were split too fine and now can't stop calling each other
Fine-grained from day one, because it always reduces total operational overhead
Neither — service granularity has no effect on cross-service call volume
mcqs.explanation: Coarse-grained services stay closer to real bounded contexts and are cheaper to split further once a specific need arises, whereas over-fine services tend to end up chatty and hard to merge back. Fine-grained-first is the reverse of the sound default, it doesn't reduce operational overhead, and granularity directly drives cross-service call volume.

mcqs.question: A company has ten services in ten separate repos, but changing Service A almost always requires changing and redeploying Service B in lockstep. What is this an example of?
options: A well-architected microservices system, since each service has its own repo
A service mesh anti-pattern specifically caused by mTLS misconfiguration
A sign that the services need to be merged into a single shared database
A distributed monolith — network overhead with none of the independent-deployability benefit
mcqs.explanation: Separate repos don't guarantee independence — if two services must deploy together, they're a distributed monolith, paying network cost without the deployability benefit that justified splitting them. This isn't a mesh/mTLS issue, and the fix is decoupling their contracts or data, not merging into a shared database (which would make coupling worse).
